title: A Letter From the Future
summary: For a creative-writing assignment, a Grade 5 boy imagines and writes a letter to himself twenty years in the future, thinking about the dreams he hopes to achieve and the person he hopes to become.
poll: Thinking about who you want to be in twenty years can help you make better choices today.

versions.title: A Letter From the Future
versions.text:
Omar likes to write. He is in Grade 5. His teacher had a plan. Kids would write a letter.

The letter was special. It was a letter to yourself. It was for many years from now!

Omar sat and thought. What could he write? He thought about his dreams.

Omar likes to build things. He fixes old toys at home. He hopes to build things when he grows up.

Mr. Khalid said, "This is just for fun. We will think about our future selves!"

Omar wrote about his dream job. He wrote about being kind, too.

He wrote, "Keep trying hard. Do not give up!"

Omar felt proud. He put his letter in a box. He can't wait to grow up!

He wrote, "Keep trying hard, even when things get tough. Never give up on your biggest dreams, no matter what happens."

versions.title: A Letter From the Future
versions.text:
Omar has always loved to write stories and poems. He is a student in Grade 5 at his school. This year, his teacher had a special plan for the whole class. Every student would write a letter. The letter was different from any they had written before.

The letter was not written to a friend. It was not written to a family member either. Instead, it was a letter written to yourself. It was meant to be read twenty years from now.

Mr. Khalid explained that this was simply a creative writing assignment. It was just a way to imagine your future self.

Omar sat at his desk and thought very hard. What in the world should he write about? He began to think carefully about the things he loved. He thought about the dreams he wanted to achieve. He also thought about the character he hoped to build.

Omar loves building things with his own two hands. He fixes old toys and small machines around his house. He often draws designs for new inventions. He hopes to become an engineer one day, someone who builds things that help people.

In his letter, Omar imagined himself twenty years older. He imagined working as an engineer. He pictured himself designing a system that brings clean water to small villages that need it.

He also wrote about the kind of person he hopes to become. He hopes to be patient, kind, and willing to help others whenever he can.

He wrote, "Keep trying hard, even when things get tough. Never give up on your biggest dreams."

Mr. Khalid collected the letters. He placed them safely inside a special box. He reminded the class that the assignment was all about imagining their hopes and goals.

Omar felt very proud once his letter was finally done. He can hardly wait to see who he becomes in twenty years. He knows that working hard today is the first step.

versions.title: A Letter From the Future
versions.text:
Omar had always been fascinated by writing stories and poems, finding real joy in letting his imagination wander freely. As a student in Grade 5 at his school, he was intrigued when his teacher announced a special assignment for the entire class.

Every student would write a letter, but this letter was unlike any they had written before: it was addressed not to a friend or a family member, but to themselves, meant to be opened and read twenty years from now.

Mr. Khalid explained that this was simply a creative writing exercise, a way for each student to envision their future self and reflect carefully on their hopes and dreams.

Before writing a single word, Omar paused to reflect on everything he loved most, the dreams he wanted to achieve, and the character he aspired to build.

Omar loves building things with his own hands, and he often repairs old toys and small machines around his house. He also enjoys sketching designs for new inventions, and he aspires to become an engineer one day, someone who builds things that genuinely help people.

Omar had chosen this particular dream for a reason. He had once encountered a news story describing children who walked for hours every day simply to find clean water, and the story had remained in his thoughts ever since.

In his letter, Omar envisioned himself twenty years older, working as an engineer who designs systems that bring clean water to small villages that do not have enough.

He also wrote about the kind of person he hopes to become: someone patient, kind, and willing to help others, understanding that perseverance would be necessary along the way.

He wrote, "Keep trying hard, even when things get tough, and never give up on your biggest dreams, no matter what happens along the way."

Mr. Khalid collected the letters and placed them safely inside a special box, reminding the class that the exercise was all about imagining their hopes and setting meaningful goals for the future.

Omar felt deeply proud once his letter was finally finished. He hoped that, whatever path he followed, he might leave some small legacy of kindness and hard work behind him.

Omar had always been fascinated by writing stories and poems, finding real joy in letting his imagination wander freely; as a student in Grade 5 at his school, he was intrigued when his teacher announced a special assignment for the entire class.

Every student would write a letter, but this letter was unlike any they had written before: it was addressed not to a friend or a family member, but to themselves, meant to be opened and read twenty years from now.

Mr. Khalid explained that this was simply a creative writing exercise, a way for each student to envision their future self and reflect carefully on their hopes and dreams; this reflection, he said, mattered more than any grade, since the point was not the writing itself but the thinking behind it.

Before writing a single word, Omar paused to reflect on everything he loved most, the dreams he wanted to achieve, and the character he aspired to build, knowing this would take real thought and more honesty than he usually offered in a school assignment.

Omar loves building things with his own hands, and he often repairs old toys and small machines around his house; he also enjoys sketching designs for new inventions, and he aspires to become an engineer one day, someone who builds things that genuinely help people.

Omar had chosen this particular dream for a reason: he had once encountered a news story describing children who walked for hours every day simply to find clean water, and the story had remained in his thoughts ever since, shaping how he imagined his future and the kind of problems he wanted to solve.

In his letter, Omar envisioned himself twenty years older, working as an engineer who designs systems that bring clean water to small villages that do not have enough, picturing the relief on the faces of people who finally had water close to home.

He also wrote about the kind of person he hopes to become: someone patient, kind, and willing to help others, understanding that perseverance would be necessary along the way, since worthwhile goals rarely come easily or quickly.

He wrote, "Keep trying hard, even when things get tough, and never give up on your biggest dreams, no matter what happens along the way."

Mr. Khalid collected the letters and placed them safely inside a special box, reminding the class that the exercise was all about imagining their hopes and setting meaningful goals for the future, not about predicting exactly what would happen.

Omar felt deeply proud once his letter was finally finished; he hoped that, whatever path he followed, he might leave some small legacy of kindness and hard work behind him, one that mattered more to him than any single achievement.

versions.title: A Letter From the Future
versions.text:
Omar, a Grade 5 student who had always found real joy in letting his imagination wander freely through stories and poems, was intrigued when his teacher, Mr. Khalid, announced a special assignment for the entire class: every student would write a letter, but this letter was unlike any they had written before, addressed not to a friend or a family member but to themselves, meant to be opened and read twenty years from now.

Mr. Khalid explained that this was simply a creative writing exercise, a way for each student to envision their future self and reflect carefully on their hopes and dreams; this reflection, he emphasized, mattered more than any grade, since the real point was the thinking behind the words rather than the words themselves. Before writing a single sentence, Omar paused to reflect on everything he loved most, the dreams he wanted to achieve, and the character he aspired to build, aware that this honest reckoning would take more thought than most assignments demanded of him.

Omar loves building things with his own hands, repairing old toys and small machines around his house and sketching designs for new inventions in his spare time; he aspires to become an engineer one day, someone who builds things that genuinely help people, a dream he had chosen for a specific reason. He had once encountered a news story describing children who walked for hours every day simply to find clean water, and the story had remained in his thoughts ever since, quietly shaping how he envisioned his future and the kinds of problems he hoped to solve.

In his letter, Omar envisioned himself twenty years older, working as an engineer who designs systems that bring clean water to small villages that do not have enough, picturing the relief on the faces of people who finally had water close to home. He also wrote about the kind of person he hopes to become: someone patient, kind, and willing to help others, understanding that perseverance would be necessary along the way, since worthwhile goals rarely arrive easily or quickly. "Keep trying hard," he wrote, "even when things get tough, and never give up on your biggest dreams, no matter what happens along the way."

Mr. Khalid eventually collected the letters and placed them safely inside a special box, reminding the class once more that the exercise was entirely about imagining their hopes and setting meaningful goals for the future, never about predicting exactly what would happen. Omar felt deeply proud once his letter was finally finished, and he hoped that, whatever path he ultimately followed, he might leave some small legacy of kindness and hard work behind him, one that mattered to him more than any single achievement ever could.

versions.title: A Letter From the Future
versions.text:
Omar, a Grade 5 student who had always found real joy in letting his imagination wander freely through stories and poems, was intrigued when his teacher, Mr. Khalid, announced a special assignment for the entire class: every student would write a letter, unlike any they had written before, addressed not to a friend or a family member but to themselves, meant to be opened and read twenty years from now.

Mr. Khalid explained that this was simply a creative writing exercise, a way for each student to envision their future self and reflect carefully on their hopes and dreams; this reflection, he emphasized, mattered considerably more than any grade, since the real point was the thinking behind the words rather than the words themselves. Before writing a single sentence, Omar paused to reflect on everything he loved most, the dreams he wanted to achieve, and the character he aspired to build, keenly aware that this honest reckoning would demand more thought and candor than most assignments ordinarily required of him.

Omar loves building things with his own hands, repairing old toys and small machines around his house and sketching designs for new inventions in his spare time; he aspires to become an engineer one day, someone who builds things that genuinely help people, a dream he had chosen for a specific and deeply personal reason. He had once encountered a news story describing children who walked for hours every day simply to find clean water, and the story had remained in his thoughts ever since, quietly shaping how he envisioned his future and the kinds of problems he hoped, one day, to solve.

In his letter, Omar envisioned himself twenty years older, working as an engineer who designs systems that bring clean water to small villages that do not have enough, vividly picturing the relief on the faces of people who finally had water close to home after years of hardship. He also wrote about the kind of person he hopes to become: someone patient, kind, and willing to help others, understanding full well that perseverance would be absolutely necessary along the way, since worthwhile goals rarely arrive easily, quickly, or without considerable setbacks. "Keep trying hard," he wrote, "even when things get tough, and never give up on your biggest dreams, no matter what happens along the way."

Mr. Khalid eventually collected the letters and placed them safely inside a special box, reminding the class once more that the exercise was entirely about imagining their hopes and setting meaningful goals for the future, never about predicting with any certainty exactly what would happen; Omar felt deeply proud once his letter was finally finished, and he sincerely hoped that, whatever path he ultimately followed, he might leave some small legacy of kindness and hard work behind him, one that mattered to him far more than any single achievement ever could.

keyWords.definition: a written message sent or kept for someone to read
keyWords.example: She mailed a letter to her grandmother.

keyWords.definition: the time that has not happened yet
keyWords.example: No one knows exactly what the future will bring.

keyWords.definition: something you hope will happen one day
keyWords.example: His dream is to travel around the world.

keyWords.definition: caring and gentle toward other people
keyWords.example: The kind boy helped his neighbor carry her bags.

keyWords.definition: to want something to happen and believe it might
keyWords.example: We hope it will not rain on the picnic.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A boy who builds a real working rocket for science class
A boy who imagines his future self and writes about his dreams
A boy who gets lost on a school field trip downtown
A boy who wins a sports contest for his school team
questions.why: The story follows Omar as he imagines his future self and writes a letter about his dreams and hopes.

wrong.A: Omar does not build a real rocket.
wrong.C: Omar does not get lost on a trip.
wrong.D: There is no sports contest in the story.

questions.stem: What did Omar's teacher ask the class to do?
options: Draw a detailed picture of their whole family
Build a small toy out of wood for the class fair
Write a letter to themselves to read twenty years later
Give a short speech in front of the entire class
questions.why: Mr. Khalid asked every student to write a letter to their future self, meant to be read twenty years later.

wrong.A: The story does not mention drawing a family picture.
wrong.B: The story does not mention building a wooden toy.
wrong.D: The story does not mention giving a speech.

questions.stem: What does Omar like to do now?
options: Build and fix things
Play soccer every day
Cook meals for his family
Sing songs in class
questions.why: The story says Omar likes to build things and fixes old toys at home.

wrong.B: The story does not mention soccer.
wrong.C: The story does not mention cooking.
wrong.D: The story does not mention singing.

questions.stem: In the story, the word future means —
options: a kind of letter that you send in the mail
a box for keeping things in a room
the time long ago, before we were born
the time that has not happened yet
questions.why: The story talks about the future as the time twenty years from now, which has not happened yet.

wrong.A: Future is not a kind of letter.
wrong.C: Future is the opposite of long ago.

questions.stem: Why does Omar want to build a water system?
options: To make his teacher happy with his science project
To help people who do not have enough clean water
To win a school prize at the end of the year
To make his toys work better in the bath
questions.why: Omar pictures himself designing a system that brings clean water to villages that need it, because he wants to help people.

wrong.A: The story does not say Omar does this to please his teacher.
wrong.C: The story does not mention a school prize.
wrong.D: The water system is not about fixing toys.

questions.stem: Why does Mr. Khalid say the letter writing is "just for fun"?
options: Because the letters are silly and nobody takes them seriously at all in class
Because no one will ever read them once they are put away in a box
Because it is not a real school lesson, so there are no marks
Because it is a game of imagining the future, not something real happening
questions.why: Mr. Khalid wants students to know this is about imagining their future, not an actual way to send something through time.

wrong.A: The story does not call the letters silly.
wrong.B: Mr. Khalid plans to keep the letters and read them later.
wrong.C: It is still a real school assignment.

questions.stem: Why does Omar write kind words to his future self?
options: Because he hopes to become a kind and patient person
Because his teacher told him exact words to write
Because he wants to win a prize for his letter
Because he is copying a letter from a book
questions.why: Omar writes about wanting to become kind and patient because that is the kind of person he hopes to be.

wrong.B: Mr. Khalid did not give exact words to copy.
wrong.C: There is no prize for the letter in the story.
wrong.D: The story does not say Omar copied a book.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell us that Omar sat and thought hard before writing?
options: To show that Omar did not like writing and wanted to stop
To explain how letters are mailed to people in other cities
To show that writing about his dreams took careful thinking
To describe Omar's classroom and the desks in it
questions.why: Showing Omar thinking hard helps readers see that writing honestly about dreams takes real effort.

wrong.B: The story does not explain mailing.
wrong.D: This detail is about Omar's thinking, not the classroom.

LOW.prompt: If you wrote a letter to yourself twenty years from now, what would you want to tell your future self? Use at least two ideas from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two ideas from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: If I wrote a letter to my future self, I would want to tell them to keep trying hard, just like Omar wrote in his letter. I would also want to tell them to be kind to other people, since Omar wrote about wanting to become a kind person. I think it would feel exciting to imagine my life twenty years from now.

keyWords.definition: to form a picture or idea of something in your mind
keyWords.example: Close your eyes and imagine a quiet beach.

keyWords.definition: a task or piece of work given by a teacher
keyWords.example: Our homework assignment was to read two chapters.

keyWords.definition: able to wait calmly without getting upset
keyWords.example: The patient nurse waited quietly for the medicine to work.

keyWords.definition: to succeed in doing something after effort
keyWords.example: She trained for months to achieve her goal of running a race.

keyWords.definition: the qualities that make up who a person really is
keyWords.example: Helping others showed everyone his strong character.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states what this story is mainly about?
options: Omar learns that writing letters is difficult and gives up
Mr. Khalid teaches the class how to mail real letters
A student imagines his future and thinks about his dreams
Omar decides engineering is too hard for him
questions.why: The story follows Omar as he writes a letter imagining his future job and the kind of character he hopes to have.

wrong.A: Omar does not give up; he finishes his letter proudly.
wrong.B: The story is not about mailing real letters.
wrong.D: Omar does not decide engineering is too hard.

questions.stem: What assignment does Mr. Khalid give the class?
options: Write a letter to their future selves, twenty years ahead
Build a model bridge for the science class and test it
Interview an engineer about their job at a company
Draw a timeline of their life with photos and dates
questions.why: Mr. Khalid asks every student to write a letter to their future self, meant to be read twenty years from now.

wrong.B: The story does not mention building a model bridge.
wrong.C: The story does not mention an interview.
wrong.D: The story does not mention a timeline drawing.

questions.stem: What dream job does Omar imagine for himself?
options: A teacher who writes letters for younger students at a school in the town
A pilot who flies passengers to many new countries on big planes
A doctor who works long hours in a big hospital in the city
An engineer who designs a system to bring clean water to villages
questions.why: Omar imagines becoming an engineer who designs systems that bring clean water to villages that need it.

wrong.A: Omar does not imagine becoming a teacher.
wrong.B: The story does not mention flying.
wrong.C: The story does not mention being a doctor.

questions.stem: In the story, the word assignment means —
options: a kind of letter sent to a close friend
a task given by a teacher for students to complete
a tool used by engineers to build bridges
a village that does not have clean water nearby
questions.why: The assignment is the task Mr. Khalid gives the class: writing a letter to their future selves.

wrong.A: An assignment is not a kind of letter itself.
wrong.C: Assignment is not an engineering tool.

questions.stem: Why does Omar think carefully about his character, not just his job?
options: Because his teacher will grade his character on the final report
Because character is easier to write about than jobs, he thinks
Because Mr. Khalid told him exactly what to say in the letter
Because he wants to become a good person, not only a successful one
questions.why: Omar writes about being patient and kind because he cares about who he becomes as a person, not only his career.

wrong.A: There is no grade for character in the story.
wrong.B: The story does not compare the difficulty of these topics.
wrong.C: Mr. Khalid did not dictate exact words.

questions.stem: What can you tell about why Omar wants to help bring clean water to villages?
options: He cares about people who face hard daily struggles
He wants to win an award for his letter
He thinks it will be an easy job
He wants to travel to as many villages as possible
questions.why: Omar's dream comes from caring about people who struggle daily without clean water nearby.

wrong.B: There is no award mentioned in the story.
wrong.C: The story does not say the job will be easy.
wrong.D: Travel is not the reason given in the story.

questions.stem: What did Omar do right before he began actually writing his letter?
options: He asked his teacher to write it for him
He thought hard about his dreams and goals
He drew a picture of a water system
He read a letter from twenty years ago
questions.why: The story says Omar sat and thought carefully before he began writing his letter.

wrong.A: Mr. Khalid did not write letters for students.
wrong.C: The story does not mention Omar drawing a picture.
wrong.D: There is no old letter in the story.

questions.stem: Why does the author include Mr. Khalid's words, "This is just for fun"?
options: To show that Mr. Khalid does not take the assignment seriously and wants the class to hurry
To explain how letters are mailed to faraway places, and how long the post takes to arrive
To make clear that the letter is an imagination exercise, not a real way to reach the future
To tell readers that the letters will be thrown away at the end of the school year
questions.why: These words remind readers that writing the letter is a thoughtful, imaginative activity, not a literal trip through time.

wrong.A: Mr. Khalid does take the assignment seriously.
wrong.B: The story is not about mailing.
wrong.D: Mr. Khalid keeps the letters safely; he does not throw them away.

MID.prompt: Explain why Omar chose to write about both his dream job and the kind of person he wants to become. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained why both ideas matter to Omar.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Omar wrote about both his dream job and his character because he wanted his future to be complete, not just successful. He imagined becoming an engineer who builds clean water systems for villages that need them, which shows his career dream. He also wrote about wanting to be patient and kind, which shows that he cares about who he becomes as a person, not only what job he has.

keyWords.definition: to think carefully about something, often about the past or oneself
keyWords.example: Before the test, she took a moment to reflect on what she had learned.

keyWords.definition: to have a strong hope or ambition to achieve something
keyWords.example: Many young scientists aspire to discover something new.

keyWords.definition: the quality of continuing to try, even when something is difficult
keyWords.example: It took great perseverance for him to finish the long race.

keyWords.definition: something a person leaves behind that continues to matter afterward
keyWords.example: The teacher's legacy lived on through the students she had inspired.

keyWords.definition: to imagine clearly what something could look like in the future
keyWords.example: The architect tried to envision how the new park would look in ten years.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the story?
options: Omar discovers that engineers never think about kindness or hard work when they plan their lives and careers in school and at home
Mr. Khalid explains how real time travel works and how a machine can take a boy like Omar to see his future life in a city
Omar decides that writing letters is a waste of time, so he stops writing to his future self and plays outside with his friends instead
A reflective student envisions his future self, weighing the career he aspires to and the character he hopes to build through perseverance
questions.why: The story centers on Omar's thoughtful reflection about both his future career and the kind of person he wants to become.

wrong.A: Omar specifically values kindness as part of his future.
wrong.B: The story frames the letter as imagination, not real time travel.
wrong.C: Omar feels proud of his letter, not that it was a waste of time.

questions.stem: What two things does Omar focus on in his letter?
options: The career he aspires to and the character he hopes to build
The grades he wants and the sports he will play in school
The house he will live in and the car he will drive one day
The friends he will have and the games he will enjoy at home
questions.why: Omar's letter focuses on his future career as an engineer and on becoming a patient, kind person.

wrong.B: The story does not mention grades or sports.
wrong.C: The story does not mention a house or a car.
wrong.D: The story does not focus on friends or games.

questions.stem: What specific problem does Omar's imagined engineering project address?
options: A shortage of school supplies
A lack of bridges between cities
A lack of clean water in small villages
A lack of electricity in large cities
questions.why: Omar envisions designing systems that bring clean water to small villages that do not have enough.

wrong.A: The story does not mention school supplies.
wrong.B: The story does not mention bridges.
wrong.D: The story focuses on villages, not large cities' electricity.

questions.stem: In the story, perseverance means —
options: giving up quickly when things are hard
continuing to try despite difficulty
a kind of engineering tool
a letter written to the future
questions.why: Omar writes that perseverance will be necessary, meaning he must keep trying even when it is hard.

wrong.A: Perseverance is the opposite of giving up.
wrong.D: Perseverance is not the letter itself.

questions.stem: What can you infer about why Mr. Khalid repeatedly frames the letter as imaginative rather than literal?
options: He thinks the students will be frightened otherwise, so he says it is only a story for fun and not for real
He does not want anyone to take the assignment seriously, so he tells them it is a game and not a grade
He is unsure whether time travel is possible, so he avoids talking about the letter as a real thing or not
He wants students to treat it as a thoughtful exercise about goals, not a real method of time travel
questions.why: By calling it "just for fun," Mr. Khalid keeps the focus on honest reflection about hopes, not on any literal journey through time.

wrong.A: There is no suggestion students would be frightened.
wrong.B: He wants students to take their reflection seriously, just not literally.
wrong.C: The story never suggests real time travel is a possibility being considered.

questions.stem: Based on the story, why might Omar's reflection on his own character matter as much as his career plans?
options: Because character is not actually important to engineers, only skill and speed matter
Because Mr. Khalid only grades character, not career plans, and he never reads the letters
Because who a person becomes shapes how they use their skills to help others
Because his classmates only wrote about careers and not about who they wanted to be
questions.why: Omar's letter suggests that being patient and kind matters because it shapes how he will use his engineering skills to help people.

wrong.A: The story suggests character matters a great deal, even for engineers.
wrong.B: There is no mention of grading in the story.
wrong.D: The story does not describe what classmates wrote.

questions.stem: Put these steps in the correct order.
options: Mr. Khalid explains the assignment → Omar thinks about his dreams → Omar writes his letter → the letters are collected
Omar writes his letter → Mr. Khalid explains the assignment → the letters are collected → Omar thinks about his dreams
The letters are collected → Omar thinks about his dreams → Mr. Khalid explains the assignment → Omar writes his letter
Omar thinks about his dreams → the letters are collected → Mr. Khalid explains the assignment → Omar writes his letter
questions.why: Mr. Khalid first explains the assignment, then Omar reflects on his dreams, writes his letter, and finally the letters are collected.

wrong.B: Omar cannot write the letter before the assignment is explained.
wrong.C: The letters cannot be collected before they are written.
wrong.D: Omar must know the assignment before he can think about what to write for it.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the story by emphasizing that today's effort shapes who Omar becomes?
options: To suggest that the future cannot be changed by anything that people do today or later
To connect the imaginative exercise to a real, practical lesson about working hard now
To hint that Omar will forget about his letter when he is grown up
To explain how engineers are paid for their work in the big companies
questions.why: This ending ties the imaginative letter-writing activity to a concrete, real lesson: effort today shapes the future.

wrong.A: The ending actually suggests the opposite: the future can be shaped.
wrong.C: There is no suggestion Omar will forget his letter.
wrong.D: The story does not discuss how engineers are paid.

HIGH.prompt: Mr. Khalid frames the letter-writing activity as something done purely for fun and imagination, not as a literal way to reach the future. Why do you think this distinction matters? Support your argument with evidence from the story.
checklist: I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think this distinction matters because it keeps the assignment grounded in something real and useful: thinking carefully about goals. If students believed the letter could literally travel through time, the exercise might feel like fantasy rather than reflection. Instead, because Mr. Khalid frames it as imagination, Omar is free to seriously reflect on the career he aspires to and the character he hopes to build through perseverance. Someone might argue that calling it "just for fun" makes the assignment seem unimportant, but treating it lightly actually makes it easier for students like Omar to be honest and thoughtful about their real hopes.
